title: Chapter 3 Review & Practice Test
overview: Pull the whole chapter together: reciprocals of linear and quadratic functions, linear-over-linear functions, rational equations and inequalities, and real-world models with holes and oblique asymptotes. Use the checklists here, then test yourself with the mixed review and practice-test questions.
objectives: Find all key features of rational functions and sketch them without technology.
Solve rational equations and inequalities and justify each step.
Write equations of rational functions from their features.
Model and analyse real situations with rational functions, including rates of change.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 at a glance
lessons.body:
| Section | Big idea | Key tool |
|---|---|---|
| 3.1 Reciprocal of a linear function | $\frac{1}{kx - c}$: one vertical asymptote, $y = 0$ | denominator $= 0$ |
| 3.2 Reciprocal of a quadratic | two, one or no vertical asymptotes; turning point at the quadratic's vertex | factor / discriminant |
| 3.3 $\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}$ | horizontal asymptote $y = \frac{a}{c}$ | divide every term by $x$ |
| 3.4 Equations and inequalities | extraneous roots; intervals | clear fractions; sign tables |
| 3.5 Making connections | holes, oblique asymptotes, models | factor & cancel; long division |

### Asymptote checklist for $f(x) = \dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$
1. **Factor** numerator and denominator; cancel common factors → **holes**.
2. Remaining zeros of the denominator → **vertical asymptotes**.
3. Compare degrees: $\deg P < \deg Q$ → $y = 0$; equal → ratio of leading coefficients; one more → **oblique** asymptote by division.
4. Zeros of the (simplified) numerator → **$x$-intercepts**; $f(0)$ → **$y$-intercept**.
5. Test points near each vertical asymptote and for large $|x|$ → **behaviour** and **end behaviour**.

lessons.title: A reliable sketching routine
lessons.body:
To sketch any rational function in this chapter without technology:

1. Find and draw the asymptotes (dashed lines).
2. Plot the intercepts and any holes (open circles).
3. Make a **sign table** using all critical values (zeros of numerator and denominator).
4. Decide the behaviour beside each vertical asymptote (does $f \to +\infty$ or $-\infty$?).
5. For reciprocals of quadratics with two zeros, plot the turning point midway between the asymptotes.
6. Join the pieces smoothly, approaching asymptotes without crossing vertical ones.

```plot
title: Example: f(x) = (x + 4)/(x − 2)
f: (x+4)/(x-2)
domain: -10, 10
range: -8, 10
points: (-4,0), (0,-2)
asymptote x: 2
asymptote y: 1
```

lessons.title: Solving: equations versus inequalities
lessons.body:
| | Equation $\frac{P}{Q} = k$ | Inequality $\frac{P}{Q} > k$ |
|---|---|---|
| Goal | specific values | intervals |
| First step | restrictions, multiply by common denominator | move everything to one side; single fraction |
| Danger | extraneous roots | multiplying by an expression of unknown sign |
| Check | substitute into the original | test a point in each interval |

**Rates of change** appear throughout: average rate = slope of a secant; instantaneous rate ≈ slope of a secant over a tiny interval.

keyTerms.definition: Where the simplified denominator is zero.
The value approached as x → ±∞ (degree comparison).
The linear quotient when the numerator's degree is one more than the denominator's.
Point discontinuity from a cancelled common factor.
A value from the algebra that does not satisfy the original equation.
A zero of the numerator or denominator used to split a number line into test intervals.

workedExamples.title: Full analysis of a reciprocal of a quadratic
steps: $y$-intercept $-\frac{1}{24}$. Turning point at $x = \frac{-3 + 8}{2} = 2.5$: $q(2.5) = -30.25$, so a local maximum $(2.5, -0.0331)$.
Increasing: $x < -3$ and $-3 < x < 2.5$. Decreasing: $2.5 < x < 8$ and $x > 8$.

workedExamples.title: Equation with a cubic
steps: $x^2 + x + 2$ has discriminant $-7$: no more real roots.

misconceptions.myth: Cancelling a common factor removes the restriction.
misconceptions.fact: The restriction stays; it becomes a hole.

misconceptions.myth: Multiply an inequality by the denominator to clear it.
misconceptions.fact: Only if you know the sign of the denominator – otherwise use a sign table or cases.
That is the $y$-intercept. The horizontal asymptote is $y = \frac{a}{c}$.

misconceptions.myth: Every reciprocal of a quadratic has a vertical asymptote.
misconceptions.fact: Not if the quadratic has no real zeros.

realWorld.title: Oil spill clean-up
realWorld.body: The cost $C(p) = \frac{50p}{100 - p}$ of cleaning up $p$% of a spill explodes as $p \to 100$ – removing the last few percent is extremely expensive.

realWorld.title: Sawmills
realWorld.body: The percent of wood lost to the saw blade, $P(t) = \frac{100t}{t + W}$, shows why thin blades matter for thick lumber.

realWorld.title: Batteries
realWorld.body: Power $P = \frac{100R}{(2+R)^2}$ peaks when the load resistance matches the battery's internal resistance.

practice.question: Write $f(x) = \dfrac{ax+b}{cx+d}$ with $x$-intercept 2, vertical asymptote $x = -1$, horizontal asymptote $y = -3$.
For $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 2}{x - 5}$, state the domain and range.

summary: Vertical asymptotes come from zeros of the simplified denominator; holes from cancelled factors.
Horizontal asymptotes come from comparing degrees; a numerator one degree higher gives an oblique asymptote.
Reciprocals of quadratics have 2, 1 or 0 vertical asymptotes depending on the discriminant.
Solve rational equations by clearing denominators and rejecting extraneous roots; solve inequalities with sign tables.
Rational models describe inverse variation, concentrations, averages and many scientific laws.

questions.text: Determine the equations of the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of each function and state each domain: (a) $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x - {{a}}}$ (b) $g(x) = \dfrac{1}{x + {{b}}}$ (c) $h(x) = -\dfrac{1}{x - {{c}}}$
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $x = {{a}}$, $y = 0$; domain $x \ne {{a}}$.

(b) $x = -{{b}}$, $y = 0$; domain $x \ne -{{b}}$.

(c) $x = {{c}}$, $y = 0$; domain $x \ne {{c}}$. (The negative sign reflects the graph but does not change the asymptotes.)

questions.text: Analyse $k(x) = -\dfrac{1}{ {{k}}x + {{c}} }$: domain, range, $y$-intercept, asymptotes, and the behaviour near the vertical asymptote. Describe the graph.
questions.modelAnswer:
Vertical asymptote ${{k}}x + {{c}} = 0 \Rightarrow x = -\frac{ {{c}} }{ {{k}} } \approx {{-c/k:3}}$; horizontal asymptote $y = 0$.

$y$-intercept $-\frac{1}{ {{c}} } \approx {{-1/c:3}}$. Domain $x \ne {{-c/k:3}}$; range $y \ne 0$.

As $x \to {{-c/k:3}}^-$ the denominator is a small negative number, so $k(x) \to +\infty$; as $x \to {{-c/k:3}}^+$, $k(x) \to -\infty$.

Graph: the reciprocal of a linear function reflected in the $x$-axis – increasing on both branches, left branch above the $x$-axis and right branch below.

questions.text: Determine the vertical asymptotes and state the domain of each function: (a) $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{(x - {{p}})(x + {{q}})}$ (b) $g(x) = -\dfrac{2}{(x + {{r}})^2}$ (c) $h(x) = \dfrac{1}{x^2 + 8x + 12}$
For $g(x) = \dfrac{1}{x^2 - 5x - 24}$: determine the asymptotes, the $y$-intercept, the local maximum, the intervals of increase and decrease, and the domain and range.
questions.modelAnswer:
$x^2 - 5x - 24 = (x - 8)(x + 3)$: vertical asymptotes $x = -3$ and $x = 8$; horizontal asymptote $y = 0$.

$y$-intercept $-\frac{1}{24} \approx -0.0417$.

Turning point at $x = \frac{-3 + 8}{2} = 2.5$; $(2.5)^2 - 5(2.5) - 24 = -30.25$, so a local maximum $(2.5, -\frac{1}{30.25}) \approx (2.5, -0.0331)$.

Increasing on $x < -3$ and $-3 < x < 2.5$; decreasing on $2.5 < x < 8$ and $x > 8$.

Domain $x \ne -3, 8$; range $y \le -0.0331$ or $y > 0$.

questions.text: Analyse $h(x) = -\dfrac{1}{x^2 - 6x + 9}$ and $k(x) = -\dfrac{1}{x^2 + {{n}}}$. For each give the asymptotes, intervals of increase and decrease, and domain and range. Explain why the graphs look so different.
questions.modelAnswer:
$h(x) = -\frac{1}{(x - 3)^2}$: vertical asymptote $x = 3$, horizontal $y = 0$. Always negative; $h \to -\infty$ at $x = 3$ from both sides. Decreasing for $x < 3$, increasing for $x > 3$. Domain $x \ne 3$, range $y < 0$.

$k(x)$: $x^2 + {{n}} \ge {{n}} > 0$, so no vertical asymptote; horizontal asymptote $y = 0$. Minimum $(0, -\frac{1}{ {{n}} })$. Decreasing for $x < 0$, increasing for $x > 0$. Domain all reals; range $-\frac{1}{ {{n}} } \le y < 0$.

The quadratic in $h$ has a double zero, giving an asymptote; the quadratic in $k$ has no real zeros, so $k$ is defined everywhere and has a minimum instead.

rubric.point: Explanation via zeros of the quadratic

questions.text:
A reciprocal of a quadratic function has these features:

* vertical asymptotes $x = -{{m}}$ and $x = {{n}}$;
* for $x < -{{m}}$ and $x > {{n}}$, $y < 0$.

Write a possible equation, state its $y$-intercept, and describe its turning point.
questions.modelAnswer:
$\frac{1}{(x + {{m}})(x - {{n}})}$ is positive outside the asymptotes, so reflect it: $f(x) = -\dfrac{1}{(x + {{m}})(x - {{n}})}$.

$y$-intercept: $f(0) = -\dfrac{1}{({{m}})(-{{n}})} = \dfrac{1}{ {{m*n}} } \approx {{1/(m*n):3}}$.

Between the asymptotes $f > 0$; the turning point is midway at $x = \frac{-{{m}} + {{n}}}{2} = {{(n-m)/2:3}}$, a **local minimum** with value $\frac{4}{({{m+n}})^2} \approx {{4/(m+n)^2:3}}$.

rubric.point: Correct equation with justification of sign

questions.text: Determine the horizontal asymptote of each function: (a) $a(x) = \dfrac{ {{p}} }{x + 5}$ (b) $b(x) = -\dfrac{ {{q}}x}{x - 3}$ (c) $c(x) = \dfrac{ {{r}}x + 2}{ {{s}}x - 2}$. Explain your method.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Numerator degree 0 < denominator degree 1: $y = 0$.

(b) $\dfrac{-{{q}}x}{x - 3} = \dfrac{-{{q}}}{1 - 3/x} \to -{{q}}$: $y = -{{q}}$.

(c) $\dfrac{ {{r}} + 2/x}{ {{s}} - 2/x} \to \dfrac{ {{r}} }{ {{s}} }$: $y \approx {{r/s:3}}$.

Method: divide each term by $x$ and let $x \to \pm\infty$ (equivalently, compare degrees and leading coefficients).

questions.text: Summarize the key features of $h(x) = \dfrac{x - {{a}}}{x + {{b}}}$ and describe its graph.
questions.modelAnswer:
Vertical asymptote $x = -{{b}}$; horizontal asymptote $y = 1$; $x$-intercept {{a}}; $y$-intercept $-\frac{ {{a}} }{ {{b}} } \approx {{-a/b:3}}$. Domain $x \ne -{{b}}$, range $y \ne 1$.

Rewrite: $h(x) = 1 - \dfrac{ {{a+b}} }{x + {{b}}}$, a reflected, stretched $\frac{1}{x}$: **increasing** on both branches. As $x \to -{{b}}^-$, $h \to +\infty$; as $x \to -{{b}}^+$, $h \to -\infty$. Branches lie top-left and bottom-right of the asymptotes' intersection $(-{{b}}, 1)$.

rubric.point: Increasing on both branches with reason

questions.text: Write an equation of the form $f(x) = \dfrac{ax+b}{cx+d}$ whose graph has an $x$-intercept of 1, a $y$-intercept of $-\dfrac{ {{r}} }{ {{q}} }$, a vertical asymptote $x = -{{q}}$ and a horizontal asymptote $y = {{r}}$. Verify every feature.
questions.modelAnswer:
Try $f(x) = \dfrac{ {{r}}(x - 1)}{x + {{q}}} = \dfrac{ {{r}}x - {{r}} }{x + {{q}}}$.

* $x$-intercept: $x - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 1$ ✓
* $y$-intercept: $f(0) = \dfrac{-{{r}}}{ {{q}} }$ ✓
* vertical asymptote: $x + {{q}} = 0 \Rightarrow x = -{{q}}$ (numerator $\ne 0$ there) ✓
* horizontal asymptote: $\frac{ {{r}} }{1} = {{r}}$ ✓

rubric.point: Verifies each of the four features

questions.text: Solve algebraically and check: (a) $\dfrac{ {{a}} }{x - {{p}}} = 2$ (b) $\dfrac{3}{x^2 + 6x - 24} = 1$
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Restriction $x \ne {{p}}$. ${{a}} = 2(x - {{p}})$, so $x = {{p}} + \frac{ {{a}} }{2} = {{p+a/2}}$. Check: $\frac{ {{a}} }{ {{a/2}} } = 2$ ✓.

(b) $x^2 + 6x - 24 = 3 \Rightarrow x^2 + 6x - 27 = 0 \Rightarrow (x + 9)(x - 3) = 0$, so $x = -9$ or $x = 3$. Neither makes the denominator zero ($81 - 54 - 24 = 3$ and $9 + 18 - 24 = 3$) ✓.

questions.text: Solve each inequality without technology and illustrate the solution on a number line: (a) $\dfrac{6}{x + 5} < 2$ (b) $\dfrac{3}{x + 2} \le \dfrac{4}{x + 3}$
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\frac{6 - 2(x + 5)}{x + 5} < 0 \Rightarrow \frac{-2x - 4}{x + 5} < 0 \Rightarrow \frac{2x + 4}{x + 5} > 0$. Critical values −5, −2. Solution: $x < -5$ or $x > -2$ (open dots at −5 and −2).

(b) $\frac{3(x+3) - 4(x+2)}{(x+2)(x+3)} \le 0 \Rightarrow \frac{1 - x}{(x+2)(x+3)} \le 0$. Critical values −3, −2, 1. Signs: +, −, +, −. Solution: $-3 < x < -2$ or $x \ge 1$ (open at −3, −2; closed at 1).

questions.text: The cost $C$, in millions of dollars, of cleaning up $p$% of an oil spill is $C(p) = \dfrac{50p}{100 - p}$. The rate of change of the cost is given by $R(p) = \dfrac{5000}{(100 - p)^2}$ (millions of dollars per percent).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the domain and range and explain them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the cost of cleaning up {{p1}}% of the spill.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Estimate the rate of change at {{p1}}% and compare with $R({{p1}})$.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Domain $0 \le p < 100$ (you cannot clean more than 100%, and the cost is undefined at 100). Range $C \ge 0$: the cost is unbounded as $p \to 100^-$.

(b) $C({{p1}}) = \dfrac{50({{p1}})}{ {{100-p1}} } \approx {{50*p1/(100-p1):3}}$ million dollars.

(c) Secant from {{p1}} to {{p1}}.01: $\dfrac{C({{p1}}.01) - C({{p1}})}{0.01} \approx {{5000/(100-p1)^2:3}}$, which matches $R({{p1}}) = \dfrac{5000}{ {{(100-p1)^2}} } \approx {{5000/(100-p1)^2:3}}$.

(d) Both the cost and its rate of change grow without bound as $p \to 100$: the last few percent of a spill are by far the most expensive to clean.

questions.text: Sketch (by describing) each function and describe each special case: (a) $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 + 5x}{x + 5}$ (b) $g(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 2x - 35}{x^2 - 3x - 28}$
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $f(x) = \dfrac{x(x + 5)}{x + 5} = x$, $x \ne -5$: the line $y = x$ with a hole at $(-5, -5)$.

(b) $g(x) = \dfrac{(x - 7)(x + 5)}{(x - 7)(x + 4)} = \dfrac{x + 5}{x + 4}$, $x \ne 7$: vertical asymptote $x = -4$, horizontal asymptote $y = 1$, $x$-intercept $-5$, $y$-intercept $\frac{5}{4}$, and a hole at $\left(7, \frac{12}{11}\right)$.

Both are special cases because a common factor cancels, producing a hole rather than an asymptote at that restriction.

questions.text: For $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x + 5}$, a student writes: 'As $x \to \infty$, $f(x) \to \infty$; as $x \to -5^+$, $f(x) \to -\infty$.' Correct each statement, justify your corrections with values, and describe the behaviour as $x \to -5^-$.
questions.modelAnswer:
As $x \to \infty$, the denominator grows without bound, so $f(x) \to 0$ (e.g. $f(995) = 0.001$), not $\infty$.

As $x \to -5^+$, $x + 5$ is a small **positive** number (e.g. $f(-4.99) = 100$), so $f(x) \to +\infty$, not $-\infty$.

As $x \to -5^-$, $x + 5$ is a small negative number ($f(-5.01) = -100$), so $f(x) \to -\infty$.

rubric.point: Corrects end behaviour with a value
Corrects behaviour from the right with a value

questions.text: State the domain and range of $f(x) = \dfrac{x + {{a}}}{x - {{b}}}$ and justify each.
questions.modelAnswer:
Domain: the denominator is zero at $x = {{b}}$, so $\{x \in \mathbb{R} \mid x \ne {{b}}\}$.

Range: the horizontal asymptote is $y = 1$; solving $\frac{x + {{a}}}{x - {{b}}} = 1$ gives ${{a}} = -{{b}}$, impossible, so $y = 1$ is never reached: $\{y \in \mathbb{R} \mid y \ne 1\}$.

questions.text: Consider $f(x) = -\dfrac{1}{x^2} + {{k}}$. Determine the domain and range, intercepts, asymptotes, and intervals of increase and decrease. Describe the graph.
questions.modelAnswer:
Domain $x \ne 0$. Vertical asymptote $x = 0$, horizontal asymptote $y = {{k}}$.

$-\frac{1}{x^2} < 0$, so $f(x) < {{k}}$: range $y < {{k}}$.

$x$-intercepts: $\frac{1}{x^2} = {{k}} \Rightarrow x = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{ {{k}} }} \approx \pm{{1/sqrt(k):3}}$. No $y$-intercept.

$-\frac{1}{x^2}$ is the reflection of $\frac{1}{x^2}$, so $f$ is decreasing for $x < 0$ and increasing for $x > 0$. Both branches plunge to $-\infty$ beside the $y$-axis and level off toward $y = {{k}}$ from below.

questions.text: If $f(x)$ is a polynomial function, does $\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$ always have a horizontal asymptote? If yes, explain why. If no, provide a counterexample.
questions.modelAnswer:
For any **non-constant** polynomial, $|f(x)| \to \infty$ as $x \to \pm\infty$, so $\frac{1}{f(x)} \to 0$: the horizontal asymptote is $y = 0$.

Counterexample: a **constant** polynomial such as $f(x) = 4$. Then $\frac{1}{f(x)} = \frac{1}{4}$ is a horizontal line; it is the graph itself, not a line approached as $x \to \pm\infty$, so it does not have a horizontal asymptote in the usual sense. (And $f(x) = 0$ gives a reciprocal that is undefined everywhere.)

So the answer is: yes for every non-constant polynomial, but not for constant polynomials.

questions.text: Solve $\dfrac{20}{x^2 - 4x + 7} = x + 2$. Give exact solutions.
questions.modelAnswer:
The denominator $x^2 - 4x + 7$ has discriminant $16 - 28 < 0$, so it is never zero: no restrictions.

Multiply: $20 = (x + 2)(x^2 - 4x + 7) = x^3 - 2x^2 - x + 14$, so $x^3 - 2x^2 - x - 6 = 0$.

Test factors of −6: $x = 3$ gives $27 - 18 - 3 - 6 = 0$ ✓. Divide: $(x - 3)(x^2 + x + 2) = 0$.

$x^2 + x + 2 = 0$ has discriminant $1 - 8 < 0$: no real roots. Solution: $x = 3$. Check: $\frac{20}{9 - 12 + 7} = 5 = 3 + 2$ ✓.

rubric.point: Finds x = 3 via the factor theorem
Shows the quadratic factor has no real roots

questions.text: Solve $\dfrac{x + 1}{x - 2} > \dfrac{x + 7}{x + 1}$ and illustrate the solution on a number line.

(a) Determine $f(x) = \dfrac{ax + b}{cx + d}$ with $x$-intercept 2, vertical asymptote $x = -1$ and horizontal asymptote $y = -{{r}}$. (b) Is it possible for a different function to have the same key features? Explain, with an example if possible.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $f(x) = \dfrac{-{{r}}(x - 2)}{x + 1} = \dfrac{-{{r}}x + {{2*r}} }{x + 1}$.

(b) Within the form $\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}$: any such function must have $\frac{a}{c} = -{{r}}$, $-\frac{b}{a} = 2$ and $-\frac{d}{c} = -1$, which forces every coefficient to be a multiple of the ones above – the same function. So no other linear-over-linear function works.

Outside that form, yes: for example $g(x) = \dfrac{-{{r}}(x - 2)(x - 5)}{(x + 1)(x - 5)}$ has the same intercept and asymptotes but also a hole at $x = 5$.

rubric.point: Gives a valid different function (e.g. with a hole)

questions.text: When a saw cuts wood, the percent of wood lost as sawdust is $P(t) = \dfrac{100t}{t + W}$, where $t$ is the thickness of the blade and $W$ the thickness of the wood (mm). Consider a {{W}}-mm-thick board.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the significance of the horizontal asymptote.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $P(t) = \dfrac{100t}{t + {{W}}}$, $t \ge 0$: starts at $(0, 0)$ and increases toward 100.

(b) Domain $t \ge 0$ (realistically $0 < t <$ a few mm); range $0 \le P < 100$.

(c) Horizontal asymptote $P = 100$: as the blade becomes enormously thick compared with the wood, almost all the wood would be lost – a limit that is never reached.

(d) $P({{t1}}) = \dfrac{ {{100*t1}} }{ {{t1+W}} } \approx {{100*t1/(t1+W):3}}\%$.

(e) $\dfrac{100t}{t + {{W}}} = {{P1}} \Rightarrow 100t = {{P1}}t + {{P1*W}} \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{ {{P1*W}} }{ {{100-P1}} } \approx {{P1*W/(100-P1):3}}$ mm.

questions.text: The acceleration due to gravity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the centre of Earth; it is 8.2 m/s² at 7000 km from the centre. (a) Write a formula. (b) Describe its graph. (c) At what distance from the centre is it {{a1}} m/s²?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show the formula and describe the graph.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $g = \dfrac{k}{d^2}$, $k = 8.2(7000)^2 = 4.018 \times 10^8$.

(b) A decreasing inverse-square curve for $d > 0$ (in practice $d \ge 6400$ km): $g \to 0$ as $d \to \infty$.

(c) $d = \sqrt{\dfrac{4.018 \times 10^8}{ {{a1}} }} \approx {{sqrt(4.018e8/a1):4}}$ km.

questions.text: Investigate the graphs of functions of the form $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x^n}$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Summarize what happens to the asymptotes and the shape (slopes) as $n$ increases, and explain the difference between even and odd $n$.
questions.modelAnswer:
For every $n$: vertical asymptote $x = 0$ and horizontal asymptote $y = 0$; all graphs pass through $(1, 1)$.

**Odd $n$** ($\frac{1}{x}, \frac{1}{x^3}, \ldots$): $f(-x) = -f(x)$, point symmetry about the origin; branches in quadrants I and III; $f \to -\infty$ as $x \to 0^-$ and $+\infty$ as $x \to 0^+$; decreasing on both branches. Through $(-1, -1)$.

**Even $n$** ($\frac{1}{x^2}, \frac{1}{x^4}, \ldots$): $f(-x) = f(x)$, symmetric about the $y$-axis; both branches above the $x$-axis; $f \to +\infty$ from both sides of 0. Through $(-1, 1)$.

**As $n$ increases:** for $|x| > 1$ the graph hugs the $x$-axis more closely (it approaches $y = 0$ faster); for $|x| < 1$ it rises more steeply near the vertical asymptote. Slopes are steeper near $x = 0$ and flatter far away.

rubric.point: Effect of increasing n on both regions

questions.text: The electric power $P$, in watts, delivered by a battery is $P = \dfrac{100R}{(2 + R)^2}$. (a) Describe the power output as $R$ increases from 0 Ω to 20 Ω, using values. (b) Show numerically that the rate of change is 0 at $R = 2$, and explain what this means.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $P(0) = 0$, $P(1) \approx 11.1$, $P(2) = 12.5$, $P(5) \approx 10.2$, $P(10) \approx 6.9$, $P(20) \approx 4.1$. The power rises quickly to a maximum of 12.5 W at $R = 2$ Ω and then decreases slowly toward 0.

(b) $\frac{P(2.001) - P(1.999)}{0.002} \approx 0$ (both values are about 12.49999). A zero rate of change at the top of the curve means $R = 2$ Ω gives the **maximum** power, 12.5 W.

rubric.point: Describes rise to max then decrease
